articles.title: My FOMO over The Duskbloods not coming to PC evaporated once I actually played it
articles.subtitle: The vampire PvPvE game is a confusing mess that isn't going to be for everyone.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
As a big Elden Ring person with an additional 600 hours in Nightreign, the FOMO of FromSoftware's next multiplayer experiment, The Duskbloods, being a Switch 2 exclusive was hitting me hard. That is, until I actually played it: I spent the majority of the closed network test held over the weekend confused about what the hell was going on, and even when I finally learned, I wasn't particularly impressed.

To be fair, the network test wasn't built to make a great first impression. It was limited to one map, six playable characters, no build customization, solo queue only, and seemed to only have a portion of its intro tutorial. I also experienced borderline unplayable input lag from the Switch 2's docked and handheld modes, which meant I was fighting the basic controls for longer than I'd like.

Assuming the final game will have all of that fixed and more, I might end up liking The Duskbloods in the end. Elden Ring Nightreign didn't click for me for close to 20 hours, and when it did, I dug it so much I spent the first half of this year playing it daily, even climbing to the highest level of its ranked mode.

The Duskbloods might reveal itself to be a masterfully created vampire multiplayer game, but as it stands right now I think it's an aimless mess of intriguing systems that don't cohere into anything worth PC gamers buying a $500 ( for now ) console for.

What does impress me is how bizarre The Duskbloods is as a videogame in 2026. At times it felt like playing a PlayStation 2 game I brought home from Blockbuster with an offbeat multiplayer mode someone cooked up before battle royales and hero shooters codified a framework for how it's done.

Tutorial popups will tell you things like, "To obtain Virtue visit Sites of Ritual to pledge yourself on the Eve of the Third Moon before the final Bestowal. " That's the kind of needlessly opaque but deliciously evocative language I love to see in a FromSoft game, but it also does absolutely nothing to prepare you for what it's like to actually play it.

The simplest way I can describe The Duskbloods is by using MOBA words. It's a game about killing creeps to level up and collect Virtue points as you prepare for the final PvP team fight (or free-for-all in solos) at the end of every match. Enemy players are there to gank you or be ganked by you as you race to become the strongest combatant in the lobby.

Otherwise, collecting Virtue is your entire goal from the moment you and seven other players drop into the map and the first round begins. The rest of the game's systems are there to disrupt you on your quest to farm as much Virtue as possible so you don't get kicked, or culled, from the match early.

Even though I expected the PvP aspect of The Duskbloods to be the worst part as someone who avoids it in FromSoft's other games, it's actually so meaningless for the majority of a match that I almost wish there was more reason to hunt down players, but it's huge risk with little reward. Dying to other players doesn't do anything but set you back on your Virtue farm. It's more lucrative to play it like you're speedrunning a normal Souls game with opportunities to PvP every now and then if you want.

On paper, the Nightreign player in me should eat that up. This is a game where everyone can triple jump and air dash like it's nothing. Over the course of my matches, however, I never fought anything that required more than your usual attack-and-dodge approach. Most monsters die in a few hits and the bosses ping-pong between players while everyone spams attacks into them until they die.

I can't tell which ones, if any, are supposed to be fodder like in a MOBA or challenging foes that reward you for memorizing their moves. At times, the hardest fight was with my eyelids, as I farmed the same mincemeat enemies over and over again. The routine is only occasionally broken by another player engaging a boss that lets everyone join under a temporary truce to help fight it.

My hope is that the final game has more of these moments that rely on having a handful of players participating.

The Duskbloods desperately needs more reasons to care about its cast of certified freaks and their unique skills that aren't purely PvP-focused. I love that I can turn it into a third-person shooter as Sniper Layla and press a button to make a gatling gun burst out of her chest, but standing still as you one-shot weak enemies gets stale real quick.

Trang Lanh's invisibility skill is largely useless against monsters who all have big attacks that'll hit you anyway, which just reduces her into a weaker melee character. Even everyone's favorite walking submarine, Zork, plays like your typical heavy-armored Souls character until other players show up and you actually have a reason to rocket yourself into them (AKA "Zorking it" ).

Recruiting enemies as allies by yelling at them until they surrender is also great, as are the unique Kin you can have by your side. I found a shirtless man named Baritone who stood by me and sang to give me a defense buff and a small snake girl inexplicably named "Gargoyle" who healed me.

You can level these weirdos up and have them tank tougher monsters for you, which ends up being pretty important as you get deeper into a match. The Kin are Elden Ring's Spirit Ash summons if they were smarter and permanent—a really fun idea that I hope future character kits can build around.

Unfortunately, the Kin feel ill-equipped for the speed of PvP fights, even sometimes sabotaging you by ruining a sneaky ambush by sprinting straight into battle.

Even with its problems, I am fascinated by FromSoft's irresistible premise: a bunch of vampires from different eras and factions fighting on the eve of an apocalypse to give themselves up to a giant moon dripping with blood. I would like to know why there is a steampunk airship in the sky and why one of the bosses looks like Bloodborne's Lady Maria riding on a headless horse.

articles.title: Hidden macOS code reveals new details about AirPods with cameras
articles.subtitle: Macworld Thanks to a video accidentally included in the macOS 26.7 beta, we got our first real confirmation that Apple is, as rumored, working on AirPods with cameras in them.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Thanks to a video accidentally included in the macOS 26.7 beta, we got our first real confirmation that Apple is, as rumored, working on AirPods with cameras in them. Despite the video and references being found in such a recent beta, we’re assured that this product isn’t actually shipping until next year.

Now, thanks to an eagle-eyed member of the MacRumors forums, we have some idea of the capabilities of the in-development AirPods with cameras. The user found a framework called “AccessorySensorManager” that provides some details of how these things might work.

First, it appears that the AirPods do not take images for you to save. Instead, they send still images in the background for Visual Intelligence to process, but nothing gets saved to your Photos app or anything like that.

The cameras seemingly operate in two modes: active and passive. Active mode is when a request is made (such as asking Siri), and each earbud captures a 640×640 image and returns a 1024×1024 processed image to your iPhone. In Passive mode, the cameras take really low-resolution 320×320 or 512×512 images at a continuous rate. While the framework focuses on standard color images, there may be other capabilities not listed, such as infrared spectrum captures.

Passive mode seems to be for background environment detection…to see if there’s a person in front of you, if you moved to a busy street, and so on. The actual camera sensors may be higher resolution, but for a variety of reasons (bandwidth, battery life, processing speed, etc.) Apple seems to be using lower-res images.

There’s mention of some processing capabilities such as lens distortion correction, dual camera calibration, and compensation for head motion. While the earbuds can take multiple images in a series, there is no video recording. The framework includes control for a hardware indicator and its brightness, which likely means that both earbuds will have some sort of recording light.

This is all subject to change, of course, especially since these AirPods aren’t expected to arrive until next fall. Test features revealed in beta frameworks are sometimes incomplete or don’t take into account later optimizations or hardware changes.

MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Wispr Flow takes on AI meeting assistants with Notetaker, its first product beyond dictation
articles.subtitle: Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

I'll be the first to admit that I have my reservations about enigmatic cryptopeddler / self-appointed anticorporate folk hero / world's most humdrum most wanted suspect Cyberleek. But I can't say their repeated leaks haven't done us all the service of answering our most burning GTA 6 questions—questions like, "If I play GTA 6, how often should I expect to confront someone who's just straight up hanging hog?"

Thanks to Cyberleek's latest illicit gameplay drop, the answer for that particular question is: Quite often, if you're frequenting one particular spot in the state of Leonida.

If you're not picking up what I'm putting down, the title of the most recent GTA 6 leak should help you with that sticky wicket: It's called "nudist_town.mp4," and it consists of the player surveying the uncensored denizens of an in-game nudist retreat—some of whom are, justifiably, unenthusiastic about being creeped on from mere feet away by a dude in work jeans with a pair of binoculars.

And when I say uncensored, I mean uncensored. We won't share the leaked video here for legal reasons, but if you seek it out yourself—it's not hard to find—you should expect to see the full spectrum of human bits and bodies matching every description except "clothed."

It's not exactly a Hot Coffee scenario, however. There's some close-proximity twerking and gyrating happening, but aside from the bared genitalia, there's really not much explicit activity going on as GTA 6 protagonist Jason takes in the scenery. There's just… a bunch of naked people standing around. I guess nudists do just as much aimless loitering as the rest of us.

Perhaps there's a lesson there. But if there is, Cyberleek doesn't appear very receptive: The video ends after they start shooting everyone because one of the nudists got mad at them for creeping too hard. Or at least, they tried to shoot everyone, and in the process dumped most of a magazine into some deck chairs. It seems Cyberleek shoots as well as they drive.

As with their previous GTA 6 leaks, nudist_town.mp4 features the expected QR code directing viewers to the cybercurrency scheme animating this whole operation. But it sounds like Cyberleek has graduated to the "making demands" stage of internet notoriety: The text watermark plastered on-screen throughout the footage says "to show support at least 10 gamers need to show up dressed as leeks in front of Take-Two / Rockstar offices holding game discs during working hours."

We'll see how that goes, I guess. Considering a YouTuber was arrested mere months ago for trespassing on the Rockstar North office premises, my expert advice would be to be normal instead. But hey, in the meantime, full dong confirmed.

articles.title: OpenAI explains what will happen when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend
articles.subtitle: It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

articles.title: 10 Perfectly Written High Fantasy Books for Fans of Lord of the Rings and Game of Thrones
articles.subtitle: Enjoy tales of wizards, assassins, and magical beasts in these imaginative stories J.R.R. Tolkien effectively established the genre of high fantasy when he came up with the world of Middle-earth and populated it with fantastical creatures facing an...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Enjoy tales of wizards, assassins, and magical beasts in these imaginative stories

J.R.R. Tolkien effectively established the genre of high fantasy when he came up with the world of Middle-earth and populated it with fantastical creatures facing an apocalyptic threat in The Lord of the Rings. While numerous stories introduce talking animals, fairies, or demons to a version of the real world — or even see regular people stepping into a magical realm they previously didn’t know existed — high fantasy takes place in a fully imaginary reality with its own rules, history, and factions.

George R. R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire proved that high fantasy doesn’t have to be synonymous with high magic. Most people in the Seven Kingdoms don’t expect to meet a dragon or giant, making it all the more terrifying when those mythical creatures appear.

The setup required to introduce a high fantasy world encourages sprawling series, but there are also brilliant standalone novels that ground their imagined worlds in real history. Whether you’re looking for an epic tale about knights and wizards, or a dangerous setting where heroes have to live by their wits, you should check out these 10 perfect high fantasy books.

Ursula K. Le Guin, A Wizard of Earthsea (1968)

One of the true masters of the genre, Ursula K. Le Guin both drew upon and subverted the classic tropes of fantasy stories. Ged, a young boy with great magical potential, has to grapple with his own impatience and hubris rather than a dark lord.

The story of a boy sent to wizarding school set the stage for Harry Potter, but A Wizard of Earthsea is a far more thoughtful tale as Ged is constantly tempted by great power but must learn to avoid easy shortcuts in order to maintain balance in himself and the world. It’s an extremely quick read, so pick up the rest of the five-book series for more beautiful and meditative stories.

Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana (1990)

Guy Gavriel Kay is known for putting fantasy spins on real history, like his heartbreakingly beautiful story of Moorish Spain The Lions of Al-Rassan. That book had almost no magic in it, so if you’re looking for more fantasy than history, you should check out Tigana, which is inspired by Renaissance Italy. The vengeful sorcerer king Brandin has erased all memory of the province of Tigana, but those who were born there must start a war to keep their home from being truly lost.

Robert Jordan, The Great Hunt (1990)

The Dragon Reborn Rand al’Thor is lost in another world with a mysterious woman who knows more than she’s letting on, while a group of aspiring Aes Sedai are betrayed and have to fend off an invasion. The Eye of the World, the first book in Jordan’s epic The Wheel of Time series, has some amazing moments, but it’s weighed down by genre cliches and its reluctant, often whiny protagonist.

But his second book, The Great Hunt, might be the best in the series, giving the characters the chance to really shine as they face numerous terrible threats.

Andrzej Sapkowski, The Last Wish (1993)

Andrzej Sapkowski began building the fantasy world of The Witcher’s Continent by putting dark spins on classic fairy tales like Beauty and the Beast and Snow White in his short story collection The Last Wish. While his Witcher novels focus more on the brutal cost of war, The Last Wish is the perfect mix of humor, action, and tragedy. The monster hunter Geralt of Rivia has to face plenty of threats from mythical creatures and cruel people, while trying his best not to get too tangled in politics.

Steven Erikson, Gardens of the Moon (1999)

Gardens of the Moon kicks off Malazan Book of the Fallen, one of the best and richest high fantasy series of all time. The Malazan Empire seeks to complete its conquest of the continent Genabackis in a conflict that involves con artists, gods, assassins, and mages. It can be hard to sink into the dense material, but if you stick with it, you’ll be rewarded with exceptionally nuanced characters and a story that can move quickly while drawing on millennia of history.

Robin Hobb, Fool’s Errand (2001)

Ideally, you’d start reading Robin Hobb at the beginning with the Farseer Trilogy, which introduces FitzChivalry Farseer, an assassin with the ability to bond with animals. But if you want to jump ahead to her best work, you can start with the Tawny Man trilogy, which picks up Fitz’s story 15 years later. That time jump allows for a more mature tale, dealing with aging and loss.
